colophon: Sarasvati Antāti, graciously composed by Kambar.

lines.1: She who grants fitting understanding of all the sixty-four arts —
lines.2: my pure Mother, radiant and crystal-clear —
lines.3: if that bright form of hers dwells within my heart,
lines.4: no misfortune will ever come near it.
lines.5: She of crystal-clear complexion and coral-red lips,
lines.6: hands like a fragrant lotus in bloom, and a waist slender as a small drum —
lines.7: if, night and day, without ceasing, one praises her,
lines.8: will not even a stone break into song?
lines.9: The glorious goddess enthroned on the white-petaled lotus, of unerring speech,
lines.10: who garlands and sways the very lotus of my mind, seated upon her own lotus throne —
lines.11: to the Lord who fashioned the earth she gave forth music; her lotus feet,
lines.12: radiant and ever bestowing grace — to those feet we bow.
lines.13: A brow curved like a bow, shoulders soft as bamboo, and upon her lovely breasts
lines.14: their fresh, natural markings, a form radiant as the rising moon, adorned with earrings,
lines.15: her wide, dark, restless eyes turned in love toward Brahma —
lines.16: O sacred threshold where penance finds its end, you who proclaim the four Vedas.
lines.17: All the branches of learning that the learned expound —
lines.18: is there, apart from you, anyone on this earth able to grant them? O one of cool, pearl-like breasts,
lines.19: you who gave me the nectar of grace and gave me life here, O gracious one,
lines.20: fragrant-tressed dweller upon the white lotus, O gentle one.
lines.21: With whatever small ability I have, to praise your sacred names
lines.22: I falter, for want of true striving — yet these three worlds themselves
lines.23: were fashioned by your very deed, O Kalaimagal; for the sake of your sacred grace,
lines.24: do not set me aside as a stranger — graciously accept and rule over even this, your servant.
lines.25: More than sunrise, shining with a beauty like moonrise,
lines.26: the beautifully adorned Lady, maiden of pure Tamil, consort of the four-faced Lord —
lines.27: she and the Lord who chants the Rig Veda ever dwell together in bliss —
lines.28: she, fragrant as a fresh-blossomed flower, the gentle peahen who rules over me.
lines.29: O peahen, O gentle young elephant, O creeper, O young doe,
lines.30: O cuckoo, O green parrot, O swan — you who dispel the fierce darkness sharp within my mind,
lines.31: O sunlight, O lightning-bright form radiant as the rising moon — henceforth
lines.32: I shall pursue no other penance; joyfully I shall worship your golden feet alone.
lines.33: To those who bow at your lotus feet you grant the many arts,
lines.34: and graciously grant Vedantic liberation too, O Bharati of the cool,
lines.35: white-petaled, fragrant lotus — may you who dwell there dwell also within my thoughts,
lines.36: for then whatever is rare to attain in this world becomes, for me, within easy reach.
lines.37: Henceforth, what I shall come to know is she of the sixty-four arts, whose lips,
lines.38: red enough to shame ripe fruit, and fair complexion, made lotus-born Brahma
lines.39: take her as his peerless consort — the Mother who brought forth the whole universe,
lines.40: the fragrant, dew-fresh-flower-dwelling one — she, the very maiden of the Vedas.
lines.41: Verse-forms and rhyme, words and metrical feet, in all their many varieties —
lines.42: the arts pertaining to them she herself ordains; the place of that ancient ordinance,
lines.43: the four ancient Vedas that her own tongue uttered, the fragrant lotus
lines.44: she dwells in, and the very minds of those who adorn her sacred feet with flowers.
lines.45: Shall I call her the new moon that dispels the sharp darkness of the mind,
lines.46: or the lamp that appears at dusk? To the good and rare Vedic sages,
lines.47: shall I call her the sun that rises at dawn's meeting-hour, or a garland of gems? —
lines.48: she, the peerless one who rests upon the shoulder of the Lord born from the navel-lotus.
lines.49: The peerless one, who gladly took her place within my otherwise empty mind —
lines.50: you who dwell upon the white lotus here, steeped in the sixty-four arts,
lines.51: you who are thought itself — so that my five senses are never led astray,
lines.52: and every thought of mine is set right by you: I shall never forget you, consort of the four-faced Lord.
lines.53: The gods, and the great divine Lord himself, who expound the four Vedas,
lines.54: the divine Trinity, and even those who have become demons, and the sages,
lines.55: everyone, and all other living beings, their lips gone pale with the effort —
lines.56: gain wisdom only through the grace of that rare Lady of the lotus.
lines.57: Entering, again and again, into the working mind, shredding away
lines.58: its darkness, and searching out the essence that all the wise seek —
lines.59: the joy that dawns clear, ripening and welling up, till the heart grows wholly lucid —
lines.60: what unfolds there is the very Veda that the deer-like Lady of the sixty-four arts herself imparted.
lines.61: The Veda, and the very culmination of the Veda, and the true reality of that culmination;
lines.62: distinction itself, and the path within that distinction, and she who resolves every dispute over that path;
lines.63: consciousness itself, having taken the very form of awareness, pervading everywhere yet utterly still;
lines.64: and the primal sound itself — O Mistress of the white lotus about which the humming bees resound.
lines.65: The sovereign abode that becomes the very heart of the lotus is the bliss born of wisdom;
lines.66: the abode that becomes the heart of another flower arises through evil deeds;
lines.67: the ever-changing abode of every living being, and
lines.68: the motherly abode of all — she herself is that white lotus, rich with pollen.
lines.69: The very lotus is her sacred temple — her hands, and the pair of her feet,
lines.70: her thighs, her sacred hip, and her navel, like a towering darkness,
lines.71: her face framed by flowing locks, her gaze, and her red lips —
lines.72: every part of her, the Goddess of Speech, measured in the mystic span of a matra and a half.
lines.73: The dark lotus, and the kaṭṭāmarai flower — these are her lovely feet;
lines.74: the rare lotus, and the red lotus — these form her very temple;
lines.75: the lotus that bestows grace, and the flawless beauty of the white lotus,
lines.76: and the great fragrant lotus — all belong to her, the doe wedded to the whole company of the arts.
lines.77: The ancient Veda, self-evident in its own meaning, taught by the four-faced Lord —
lines.78: this became, for me, a sacred consecration in itself. The gods themselves
lines.79: call it the remedy that dispels sorrow of mind; I call it the flower I wear upon my head —
lines.80: for it is nothing but the lotus feet of thick-tressed Kalaimangai.
lines.81: She who dwells upon the lotus — those who lovingly join their hands there in worship,
lines.82: she whom even the lotus-born gods themselves praise, my beauteous one — the grace within her eyes,
lines.83: that very lotus, if one takes as one's focus, beholding it once and holding it firm in mind,
lines.84: one shall pass beyond the bonds of this worldly life — O Kalaimangai, Vedic-adorned, primal Cause of all.
lines.85: She who is half the body of the primal Cause, and who dwells upon his crown, and the maidens who accompany them;
lines.86: Lakshmi, who never departs from Narayana's chest, and she seated upon the four-tusked elephant;
lines.87: the consort of Indra, and all the other divine ladies —
lines.88: all of them are but servants carrying out the command of the Vedic Maiden.
lines.89: Her feet are fragrant with the Vedas — for all the glorious Vedas
lines.90: she is the very culmination, O lightning-splendor upon the white lotus; of the never-ending vow,
lines.91: she is the very embodiment for those who joyfully worship her; through the night of delusion,
lines.92: she alone is the dawning knowledge that rules over me — in this whole world there is no other refuge.
lines.93: Knowing there is no other refuge, I have joined the ranks of your devotees, praising your glorious name;
lines.94: though I am unworthy, I have stood fixed upon you — let not the mischievous five senses,
lines.95: those unfailing thieves, lead me into delusion on the path of your flower-feet —
lines.96: graciously grant me a path free of mire, O red-jeweled one enthroned upon the white lotus.
lines.97: The paths of logical disputation that can be demolished, and the thoughts of every kind of thinker,
lines.98: can be tested and thoroughly taught; and having settled firmly upon what is taught,
lines.99: one can accomplish it, discern it with full clarity, and attain liberation itself —
lines.100: for those who have taken refuge at the golden feet of that peahen-Lady, mistress of all these arts.
lines.101: The fresh flower that is her emblem, the palm-leaf book in her hand, and a string of gems —
lines.102: she who holds these, she of a waist so slender it seems scarcely to exist, she who is the very essence of the Upanishads,
lines.103: whose power creates every living being, she who wears the fragrant
lines.104: lotus garland — other than her, whom else should I ever worship?
lines.105: Those who worship her, circle round her, and praise her, forgetting their own work;
lines.106: those who fall prostrate before her, those who discern the true essence of the rare Vedas, their bodies thrilling with joy;
lines.107: those who embrace her, and those whose eyes well with tears — what, then, of me, who has done none of this?
lines.108: Only those who have truly set their love upon the unfailing, true-worded Kalaimangai know this blessing.
lines.109: The wealth one stores away, the wealth of household life, and every other kind of wealth —
lines.110: none of these, on this earth, are things that endure; they are nothing but things fated to prove false;
lines.111: the one substance that is truly real, that never perishes, the noblest of all substances,
lines.112: the substance that leads to true deliverance — that is the very essence taught by the deer-like Lady of the arts.
lines.113: The notion that both worldly and spiritual good can be won through mere wealth — is that truly the substance of things?
lines.114: Or is the unerring art of her speech itself the supreme substance? That substance, once reverently sought,
lines.115: shines forth as grace, as very light, to those devotees — while to those who do not know it,
lines.116: it appears only as darkness. O radiant-jeweled one, whose form gleams with goodness.
lines.117: Her radiant, sacred face — when a thrill runs through the body and tears well in the eyes,
lines.118: when the senses grow overwhelmed, and flawless speech comes to fruition, the mind stirred exceedingly,
lines.119: as her radiant smile forms, joy surges like a swirling stream —
lines.120: yet even at that moment of turbulence, clarity dawns, for those who meditate upon the Deer-Lady of Speech.
lines.121: Her dark, dense tresses, her eyes, the radiant, jeweled tips of her breasts, and her lovely,
lines.122: well-formed hands, her feet, her lips, and her fair, fragrant,
lines.123: many-whorled lotus, her sacred form, and every ornament she wears —
lines.124: all these stand fixed, without ever departing, in my heart and upon my tongue, O great and glorious one.
lines.125: She who is both great splendor, and the Lady of Victory, who graciously dwells
lines.126: within my simple heart — the true-worded, vine-slender Lady — if one praises her, then to all living beings
lines.127: she grants fitting wisdom, and grants also the blissful essence of the Vedas,
lines.128: she grants refined wealth, and grants imperishable, great glory besides.
